title: The Jordan–Chevalley–Dunford Decomposition
description: Proves the Jordan–Chevalley–Dunford decomposition: every endomorphism f of a finite-dimensional vector space over a perfect field splits as f = s + n, where s is semisimple, n is nilpotent, s and n commute, and both are polynomial expressions in f. The decomposition is shown to be unique. This is the basis-free shadow of the Jordan canonical form studied in the parent entry, and unlike that entry it is fully machine-checked with no axioms, via Mathlib's Newton-iteration proof together with the fact that a difference of commuting semisimple operators is semisimple.

meta.assumptions: None beyond Mathlib. The results are fully machine-checked over an arbitrary perfect field K and a finite-dimensional K-vector space V; #print axioms reports only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The existence half (the decomposition itself) is obtained via Mathlib's Newton-iteration theorem Module.End.exists_isNilpotent_isSemisimple, and uniqueness is assembled from Mathlib's IsSemisimple.sub_of_commute and eq_zero_of_isNilpotent_isSemisimple; this file contributes the explicit polynomial-in-f witnesses, the commutation lemmas, and the packaged ExistsUnique statement (which Mathlib leaves as a TODO).

overview.historicalContext: The decomposition is due to Camille Jordan and was put in its modern operator-theoretic form by Claude Chevalley (Théorie des groupes de Lie, 1951) and Nelson Dunford (in the analytic/spectral setting). It refines the Jordan canonical form (Jordan, 1870): rather than choosing a Jordan basis, one decomposes the operator itself into a commuting sum of a semisimple (diagonalizable over the algebraic closure) part and a nilpotent part, both of which are polynomials in the operator. Existence requires the ground field to be perfect; over a non-perfect field the semisimple part may fail to be a polynomial in f.
overview.problemStatement: Can every linear endomorphism f of a finite-dimensional vector space over a perfect field be written as f = s + n with s semisimple, n nilpotent, [s, n] = 0, and both s and n polynomials in f? Is the decomposition unique?
overview.text: We answer YES on both counts. Existence comes from Mathlib's Module.End.exists_isNilpotent_isSemisimple, which proves the decomposition by Newton's method (following Chambert-Loir): the nilpotent and semisimple parts are produced inside the subalgebra adjoin K {f} = K[f], so they are automatically polynomials in f and automatically commute. We extract the explicit polynomial witnesses and the commutation. For uniqueness, if f = s₁ + n₁ = s₂ + n₂ are two such decompositions, then s₁ - s₂ = n₂ - n₁; the left side is semisimple (a difference of commuting semisimple operators over a perfect field, IsSemisimple.sub_of_commute) and the right side is nilpotent (a difference of commuting nilpotents), so it is both semisimple and nilpotent, hence zero. Thus s₁ = s₂ and n₁ = n₂.
overview.proofStrategy: Wrap Mathlib's Newton-iteration existence result; extract commutation and polynomial-in-f witnesses from membership in adjoin K {f}; prove uniqueness from eq_zero_of_isNilpotent_isSemisimple combined with the closure of commuting semisimple operators under subtraction.
keyInsights: Working inside the commutative subalgebra K[f] = adjoin K {f} makes both the commutation [s, n] = 0 and the 'polynomial in f' clause automatic.
Uniqueness reduces to a single fact: an operator that is simultaneously semisimple and nilpotent is zero — applied to s₁ - s₂ = n₂ - n₁.
The perfect-field hypothesis is exactly what makes a difference of commuting semisimple operators semisimple (IsSemisimple.sub_of_commute), which is the new Mathlib ingredient enabling uniqueness.

Existence is genuinely constructive: Mathlib's proof runs a Newton/Hensel-type iteration (following Chambert-Loir) entirely inside K[f], so the semisimple and nilpotent parts emerge as honest polynomials in f rather than as abstract spectral projections.

The result is the basis-free refinement of the Jordan canonical form: rather than choosing a Jordan basis, one decomposes the operator itself — and unlike the parent entry's axiomatized Jordan-form/minpoly relationship, this additive splitting is reached with 0 axioms over any perfect field.
prerequisites: Minimal polynomial and the subalgebra K[f] generated by an operator
Newton's method / Hensel-type lifting (used inside Mathlib's existence proof)

conclusion.summary: The Jordan–Chevalley–Dunford decomposition is formalized with 0 axioms: existence (with commuting parts exhibited as polynomials in f) and uniqueness, packaged as an ExistsUnique statement. 5 theorems, 129 lines.
conclusion.implications: This is the operator-theoretic core of spectral theory and the structure theory of linear algebraic and Lie groups. Whereas the parent entry (cayley-hamilton-minpoly-oq-01) needed three structural axioms to reach the Jordan-form/minpoly relationship, this basis-free formulation is fully verified, demonstrating that the semisimple+nilpotent splitting is accessible without axiomatizing the Jordan normal form.
openQuestions: Generalize existence beyond perfect fields by hypothesizing only that some separable polynomial annihilates a power (the separable/p-th-power obstruction).
Relate the multiplicative analogue (unipotent × semisimple, the multiplicative Jordan decomposition) for invertible f.
Connect the additive parts here to the explicit Jordan-block exponents of the minimal polynomial from the parent entry.

sections.title: Header: The Jordan–Chevalley–Dunford Decomposition
sections.summary: States the open question — can every linear endomorphism f of a finite-dimensional vector space over a perfect field be written as f = s + n with s semisimple, n nilpotent, s and n commuting, and both polynomials in f, uniquely? Answers yes on both counts: this is the coordinate-free, basis-independent shadow of the parent entry's Jordan canonical form, obtained here fully machine-checked and axiom-free via Mathlib's Newton-iteration existence proof and a perfect-field uniqueness argument built from commuting semisimple elements of K[f].
sections.mathContext: Existence comes from Mathlib's $\mathrm{Module.End.exists\_isNilpotent\_isSemisimple}$ (Newton's method); uniqueness from $\mathrm{IsSemisimple.sub\_of\_commute}$, the missing ingredient Mathlib lists as a TODO at the packaged $\mathrm{ExistsUnique}$ level, supplied here.

sections.title: Polynomials in f commute
sections.summary: Any two elements of the subalgebra K[f] = adjoin K {f} are polynomials in f and therefore commute; in particular each commutes with f. This supplies the commutation clause [s, n] = 0 for free.
